catalog_quote: [p.2] Contrastive contour tones are a salient feature of Kakua’s phonology. ... Primary stress is assigned to the first syllable of the leftmost root of the word, and a secondary stress is assigned to the last syllable of the last element of the word. ... [p.3] The language is predominantly suffixing, with a few prefixes occurring exclusively on the verb. ... [p.70] Based on my data, I propose that Kakua displays a tonal inventory of 3 contrastive phonological tones: LH [rising] (/LH/ [LH]), HL [falling] (/HL/ [HL]), and L [low] (/L/ [L]). The analysis presented in this section is still in progress and should be taken as preliminary. ... [fn.16, p.71] Pitch, accent, and stress is not described in this phonological description of Kakua, primarily because of the limitations on providing a robust analysis of these phonological phenomena. ... audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every segment of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the LOT 433 PDF we hold at the stated printed pages (p.2, p.3, p.70, fn.16 p.71). (2) Deciding source is the 2016 reference grammar (393 pp), the top item in Glottolog's bibliography and the most recent description; no later prosodic/instrumental study of Kakua was found. (3) The two earlier phonology works Glottolog lists (Cathcart 1979 SIL; Bolaños 2010 MA) were not yet obtained; both were downloaded now (the Internet Archive), and read. Both agree with the catalog's substance — prominence is assigned within the base/root, pre-base proclitics/prefixes are unaccented ('function morphemes are transparent', 2010 p.80; accent 'cae sobre.. la base', 1979 p.37) — so the set by morphology (root-referring, non-strict) classification stands. sources.citation: Bolaños Quiñónez, Katherine Elizabeth. 2010. Kakua phonology: first approach. MA thesis, University of Texas at Austin. 133 pp. (UT repository handle 2152/ETD-UT-2010-12-2485)
sources.quote: p.79: 'Kakua presents a word-level prominence whereby the first high syllable closest to the right [sic] edge of the word is assigned more prominence. This functions as an intonation pattern to demarcate word boundaries. Syllabic prominence is not contrastive and for that reason I have chosen to analyze Kakua as a tonal language without contrastive interaction with a stress pattern.' ... 'The Kakua word-level prominence pattern assigns a primary prominence to the first syllable that at the left-most edge bears the highest pitch in the phonological word. A weak secondary word-level prominence a
sources.note: Fullest discussion of Kakua word prominence (§3.2.1, pp.79-81), which the 2016 grammar compresses to one sentence on p.2 and a footnote; states root-only prominence with prefixes transparent, leftmost highest-pitch syllable, non-contrastive/demarcative.

sources.citation: Cathcart, Marilyn E. 1979. Fonología del cacua. In: Sistemas fonológicos de idiomas colombianos 4, pp. 9-45. Lomalinda: Editorial Townsend / Instituto Lingüístico de Verano. (SIL archive 18887)
sources.quote: p.11: 'El tono y la nasalización, más que el acento, son los rasgos distintivos del pie en la lengua cacua.' p.37: 'La palabra fonológica se caracteriza por tener una sílaba nuclear ligeramente acentuada y una pausa potencial al final. Mientras que el acento no siempre es perceptible o predecible, parece que cae sobre la primera sílaba más alta de la base — en el caso anterior sobre /pia²/ "dar la vuelta".' §5: phrase-level accent tends to fall on the second word; word/phrase accent elsewhere 'no han sido completamente analizados todavía'. Tone inventory given as 4 tones (differs from Bolaños'
sources.locator: book p.11 (p.18) and §4 'Nivel de la palabra fonológica', book p.37 (p.44; page scan checked visually)
sources.note: Only pre-Bolaños phonology of Cacua; gives the earliest explicit word-accent statement (weak accent on first highest-toned syllable of the base) — independent support that pre-base proclitics are unaccented and that accent is tone-conditioned within the base.

sources.note: Silent on word stress: the catalog record (Bolaños 2016: primary stress on the first syllable of the leftmost root, secondary on the last syllable of the word; three contrastive contour tones) is neither confirmed nor contradicted. The footnote's tonal remark ('tone (four levels)' with the phonological foot as domain, written high-slow-downglide / high-fast-downglide / mid / low) is an earlier SIL analysis of the tone system that differs in inventory from Bolaños's three contour tones; it concerns tone, not stress placement, and matches the foot-based prosody analysis of Cathcart 1979 already…
